    22nd Physics of Estuaries and Coastal Seas (PECS 2026)
    
      SWPECS 2026 conference photo forthcoming
      Portland, Maine · August 9–14, 2026
    
    Kimberly Huguenard helped facilitate PECS 2026, with SWELL Lab members helping run the conference in Portland, Maine.
    The conference took place from Sunday, August 9, through Friday, August 14, 2026, at Hannaford Hall at the University of Southern Maine. PECS brings coastal engineers and oceanographers together to exchange research on estuaries and coastal seas, with opportunities for students and early-career researchers to connect with the wider community.
    Topics included tides and waves, sediment transport, river–coast interactions, and estuaries under climate change.
    Visit the official PECS 2026 conference page for the program and further details.

Reading the coast.From individual currents to coastal systems, we investigate how water moves—and what that movement means for a changing shoreline.Flooding ↘Estuaries ↘Resilience ↘Research activities ↘
  Flood: inland ← · Ebb: seaward → · Slack: still water
  Pause tides


Research overview: draft for lab review.
01
          
          
          
          
        Storms &coastal floodingStorm surge, tides, and river flows interact to influence coastal flooding. We investigate these connections to better understand how extreme events affect estuaries and nearby communities.Storm surgeTidesCompound floodingThe driving questionWhen do storms, tides, and rivers combine to raise water levels?
02
          
          
          
          
        Estuariesin motionWhere rivers meet the ocean, circulation and mixing shape the water’s structure. Field observations help us investigate turbulence, river plumes, and the exchange of fresh and salt water.CirculationTurbulenceMixingThe driving questionHow do fresh and salt water move, mix, and exchange?
03
          
          
          
          
          
        ResilientcoastlinesCoastal science also informs practical decisions. Our broader research interests connect hydrodynamics with living shorelines, aquaculture systems, and marine renewable energy.Living shorelinesAquacultureOffshore windThe driving questionHow can understanding coastal processes inform coastal decisions?

  Research in practiceOn the water. In the lab. Together.Our research connects field measurements, sample analysis, and shared learning. Here is how we collect observations and bring coastal science into conversation.
  
    
      Preparing an instrument frame on the water.
      Measure currentsADCP deployments & data processingWe deploy acoustic Doppler current profilers (ADCPs) and process the observations to investigate currents and estuarine circulation.
    
    
      Working with instruments and a laptop aboard the field boat.
      Across the estuaryADCP transectingBoat-based transects let us observe how conditions vary across an estuary. Transecting complements our instrument deployments and connects measurements from different parts of the system.
    
    
      Handling a sampling line from the field boat.
      Through the water columnmicroCTD & Eureka probe castsOur field activities include microCTD casts and Eureka probe casting. These observations complement current measurements as we study conditions through the water column.
    
    
      Sampling supplies ready for a day on the river.
      From field to labSediment & PFAS samplingWe collect water samples containing suspended sediment using Niskin bottles, process sediment samples in the lab for organic and inorganic components, and carry out PFAS sampling.Suspended-sediment sampling with Niskin bottlesLaboratory processing of organic and inorganic sedimentPFAS sampling
    
    
      Workshop space at the University of Maine IMRC Center in Orono, August 5, 2025.
      Collaborative modelingConnecting Estuarine Dynamics and Fish MigrationCollaborative Modeling of Mercury Exposure in the Penobscot RiverThis full-day workshop at the University of Maine's IMRC Center was designed to bring together community members, researchers, and Tribal members to explore how tidal dynamics, fish behavior, and mercury contamination intersect in the Penobscot River Estuary.In partnership with the Penobscot Nation, the workshop focused on identifying biological processes and environmental conditions that shape contaminant exposure in sea-run fish. Hands-on modeling and discussion centered on integrating ecological knowledge, community input, and Tribal priorities into model development.Identify behavioral and environmental drivers of mercury exposureRefine ecological model components through interdisciplinary and community perspectivesIdentify model outputs and simulations relevant to participants' interestsOrganized by Vanessa Quintana, Gayle Zydlewski, Katrina Armstrong, and Todd Swannack.
    
    
      Sharing coastal research at the Maine Sustainability & Water Conference in Augusta, March 26, 2026.
      Share the scienceConference participationWe shared coastal research at the 2026 Maine Sustainability & Water Conference, held at the Augusta Civic Center on March 26. Poster sessions, presentations, and discussion connect our work with the wider research community. We also participate in the Physics of Estuaries and Coastal Seas (PECS) conference.Read about SWELL at PECS 2026 ↗
    
  

The approachObserve. Understand. Connect.Field measurements provide a close look at coastal processes. Working across disciplines helps connect those observations to questions facing coastal communities.The research themes above draw on Dr. Huguenard’s University of Maine research profile. The activities highlight our work in the field, in the lab, and with the research community.Discuss a collaboration ↗

  Principal investigatorDr. KimberlyHuguenardSWELL Lab · University of MaineResearch biography forthcoming.kimberly.huguenard@maine.eduContact Kim ↗

The teamOur researchers.
  
    Postdoctoral researcherDr. Vanessa Mahan QuintanaDr. Vanessa Mahan Quintana is a postdoctoral researcher in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Maine. Her research integrates field observations, hydrodynamics, and individual-based modeling to understand how interacting physical, biological, and behavioral processes shape ecological patterns and environmental risk.Her work focuses particularly on contaminant fate and exposure in aquatic and estuarine systems, including mercury and PFAS, and on developing reusable ecological modeling approaches for research and decision support.She earned her Ph.D. in Marine Biology from the University of Maine in 2026 under the guidance of Dr. Kimberly Huguenard in the School of Marine Sciences.vanessa.mahan@maine.edu
    PhD Candidate in Civil Engineering, University of MaineNalika LakmaliNalika Lakmali is a researcher with interests in estuarine tidal hydrodynamics, tide-surge interactions, and numerical modelling of nearshore coastal processes. She earned her bachelor’s degree in Earth Resources Engineering and her master’s degree in water resources engineering and management from the University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka. Her research aims to inform and support the sustainable management of global coastal and inland water resources (Google Scholar, LinkedIn).engiliyage.nalika.lakmali@maine.edu
    PhD studentNicolas CyrNick Cyr is a coastal engineering researcher specializing in cold-region estuarine hydrodynamics and large-scale observational field studies.His doctoral research examines physical processes in estuarine systems using measurements of currents, waves, salinity, density, and internal wave and current phenomena, with particular experience in the Penobscot River and Bay.He completed his M.E. and B.S. degrees in Civil and Environmental Engineering, focusing on water resources and coastal engineering, and expects to complete his PhD in 2027.nicolas.cyr@maine.edu
    PhD studentMalavika Sudhakaran, PhD Researcher in Civil and Environmental EngineeringMalavika Sudhakaran is a Ph.D. Researcher in Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Maine. Her research focuses on coastal hydrodynamics, particularly nonlinear wave-tide-surge interactions and their influence on water levels and coastal circulation. She uses the hydrodynamic model, Delft3D to investigate coastal processes and storm-driven dynamics at the Kennebec coast and is also involved in field monitoring of waves, currents, and water levels at living shoreline sites along the Maine coast. She earned her master’s degree in physical Oceanography from Cochin University of Science and Technology, India, in 2019.malavika.sudhakaran@maine.edu
    Master’s studentSasha Bugbee, M.S. Civil EngineeringSasha Bugbee is a graduate student pursuing her M.S. in Civil Engineering at the University of Maine. Her research focuses on using observational turbulence data to understand the hydrodynamics of the Kennebec River Estuary. Prior to graduate school, she was an undergraduate research assistant at the University of Washington, where she instrumented the Willapa River Estuary to examine coastal flooding response and provide data for local stakeholders. She earned her B.S. in Civil Engineering there, with an emphasis in riverine and coastal engineering.sasha.bugbee@maine.edu
